fields.h1: Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions: A Study Guide to the Standard Sermons
fields.meta_title: Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions — Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A reader’s study guide and summary of John Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions — the doctrinal standard of Methodism. Which sermons to read first, the central themes, and how to read the whole collection.
fields.body_html:
If you want the clearest single window into what early Methodism actually believed — not the caricature, but the settled teaching — you open John Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions. This is the collection the movement adopted as its doctrinal yardstick. When Methodist preachers were licensed, they promised to teach nothing contrary to Wesley’s Standard Sermons and his Notes on the New Testament. That gives this book an unusual weight: it is not merely a great preacher’s greatest hits, but the agreed measure of a whole tradition’s message. This study guide is your orientation to it — what the collection is, which sermons to read first, the handful of themes that run through everything, and how to work through a book this large without losing your way.

What the collection is, and why it became a doctrinal standard

Wesley preached for more than fifty years, often in the open air, to coal miners and gentry alike, and he wrote as he preached: plainly, warmly, and to be understood. Over his lifetime he gathered the sermons he most wanted preserved into successive volumes titled Sermons on Several Occasions. The Ochorus edition brings the full sweep together — the early university sermons that first drew fire, the great salvation discourses of the revival, the long series on the Sermon on the Mount, and the later reflective pieces on providence, eternity, and the life to come.

What sets these apart from ordinary sermon literature is their doctrinal function. Wesley did not write systematic theology; he did his theology from the pulpit, tethered always to a text. So the sermons carry the doctrine, and because Methodism named them its standard, they carry it authoritatively. If you have ever wondered what Wesley meant by justification, the new birth, assurance, or Christian perfection, the answers are here in his own words, worked out with pastoral care rather than debated in the abstract. His opening sermon sets the key that never changes:

All the blessings which God hath bestowed upon man are of his mere grace, bounty, or favour; his free, undeserved favour; favour altogether undeserved; man having no claim to the least of his mercies.John Wesley

How the collection is organized, and where to begin

Do not start at page one and try to march to the end. A collection of more than fifty sermons rewards a reader who begins with the landmarks and lets them open the rest. The volume moves, broadly, from the foundations of salvation, through the marks and means of the Christian life, into the long meditation on the Sermon on the Mount, and finally to the wider works of God. A good first path through it is this:

  • Salvation by Faith — the manifesto, preached at Oxford in 1738 on By grace are ye saved through faith (Ephesians 2:8). Begin here; everything else grows from it.
  • The Almost Christian — Wesley’s searching contrast, on Acts 26:28, between the person who has the form of religion and the one who has its living power.
  • Scriptural Christianity — preached before the University of Oxford on Acts 4:31, tracing what real Christianity looks like when the Spirit fills a people.
  • The Scripture Way of Salvation — his mature, orderly summary on Ephesians 2:8, the best one-sermon overview of how a person is saved.
  • Christian Perfection — the doctrine most associated with Wesley, patiently explained and defended from Philippians 3:12.
  • Free Grace — his forthright sermon on Romans 8:32, insisting that Christ died for all.

Once those six are in hand, branch outward as your interest leads: The Means of Grace (Malachi 3:7) on prayer, Scripture, and the Lord’s Supper; Catholic Spirit (2 Kings 10:15) on loving Christians who differ from you; The Use of Money (Luke 16:9) on Wesley’s famous counsel to gain, save, and give all you can; and the great thirteen-discourse series on our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, which is a book within the book.

The central themes that run through everything

For all its breadth, the collection returns again and again to four convictions. Hold these four and you hold Wesley.

Justification by faith

Wesley is relentlessly clear that we are accepted by God not on the ground of anything we do, but through faith in Christ. Human works, however many or apparently holy, cannot atone for sin, because even our best deeds are God’s gift and are themselves stained. In The Scripture Way of Salvation he reduces the whole of Scripture to two words:

These two little words, I mean faith and salvation, include the substance of all the Bible, the marrow, as it were, of the whole Scripture.John Wesley

This is the Reformation gospel, and Wesley preached it without flinching (see Romans 3:28). But he never let it stand alone, which brings us to the other three themes.

The witness of the Spirit and assurance

Wesley believed a Christian could know, not merely hope, that he is a child of God. Several sermons — The Witness of the Spirit, The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption, The Marks of the New Birth — unfold the doctrine of assurance from texts such as Romans 8:16, where the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are the children of God. This inward testimony, tested by the outward fruit of a changed life, was one of the great recoveries of the revival, and it is worked out here with unusual pastoral balance: real, but not to be presumed upon.

Sanctification and Christian perfection

Wesley’s most distinctive and most misunderstood teaching is that God intends to make believers actually holy in this life — not merely to declare them righteous but to purify the heart in love. He knew the word perfect provoked people, and he refused to drop it because Scripture uses it:

Whatsoever God hath spoken that will we speak, whether men will hear or whether they will forbear.John Wesley

By perfection Wesley did not mean freedom from ignorance, mistake, or temptation, but a heart so filled with love for God and neighbour that sin no longer reigns — the fulfilment of the command to love God with all the heart, and one that reaches beyond the mere refraining Jesus warns against in Matthew 5:20. Christian Perfection and On Perfection are the key sermons; the doctrine is expanded at book length in his A Plain Account of Christian Perfection.

Free grace

Wesley preached, against the Calvinism of some of his closest friends, that God’s saving love is offered to every person without exception. The sermon Free Grace, on Romans 8:32, is his warm and controversial statement of it, and God’s Love to Fallen Man (Romans 5:15) turns even the fall of Adam toward the mercy that answers it. Wesley opens the argument with a cry rather than a syllogism:

How freely does God love the world! While we were yet sinners, Christ died for the ungodly.John Wesley

Who should read it

This collection is for more readers than you might expect. If you are a Methodist, or in any church shaped by the Wesleyan tradition — Nazarene, Free Methodist, holiness, or much of Pentecostalism — this is your family’s founding charter, and reading it is like meeting a great-grandparent whose features you recognize in yourself. If you are a preacher or teacher, Wesley is a master class in clear, text-anchored, pastoral proclamation that never talks over ordinary people. If you are simply a Christian who wants a sturdy, joyful account of the gospel — how a person is saved, how they can know it, and how God means to make them holy — you will find few better guides. And if you are a student of the eighteenth-century revival, these are the very documents that carried its theology into a movement that reshaped the English-speaking world.

You do not need a seminary background. Wesley’s eighteenth-century English is dignified but plain, and he defines his terms as he goes. A reader willing to slow down for a few older words will follow him easily.

How to read it today

A collection this large is best approached as a well-stocked library rather than a novel. A few practical habits make it a pleasure instead of a burden:

  1. Read one sermon at a sitting. Each is a complete, self-contained argument built on a single verse. Finish one before you begin the next, and you will never feel lost.
  2. Follow the six landmarks first (listed above), then wander by theme. Let Salvation by Faith and The Scripture Way of Salvation give you the frame before you explore the corners.
  3. Read with the text open. Wesley preaches on a verse and stays close to it. Keeping Ephesians 2:8, Philippians 3:12, or 1 John 3:9 in front of you turns each sermon into a Bible study.
  4. Watch his numbered structure. Wesley almost always announces his divisions — First, Secondly — so if you lose the thread, scan for the next numbered head and rejoin him there.
  5. Do not rush the Sermon on the Mount discourses. Thirteen sermons on Matthew 5, 6, and 7 form a unit; read them as a short course over several weeks rather than in one push.
  6. Pair it with the fuller treatments. When a theme grips you, follow it into a whole book — Wesley’s own A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, or the devotional classic that shaped Wesley himself, William Law’s A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life.

Read this way, over a season rather than a weekend, the collection becomes what it was for the first Methodists: not a monument to be admired but a living standard to be tested against and formed by. You can read the full text free on Ochorus, and explore more of the man behind it on John Wesley’s author page.

For reflection

Whether you are reading alone, with a friend, or in a group, these questions carry the collection’s heart into your own life:

  • Wesley distinguishes the almost Christian from the altogether Christian. Reading his description, which more honestly describes you today — and what would move you from one to the other?
  • Wesley insists a believer may know, by the witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), that he is God’s child. Have you settled the question of assurance, or do you still live in the spirit of bondage he describes?
  • The doctrine of Christian perfection troubles many readers. Before dismissing it, can you state what Wesley actually means — and what he does not mean — by a heart made perfect in love?
  • Wesley preached that grace is free for all (Romans 8:32). How does that conviction change the way you pray for the people you are most tempted to write off?
  • In The Use of Money Wesley urges believers to gain all they can, save all they can, and give all they can (Luke 16:9). Which of the three do you find hardest, and why?
